sentences.text: The species M. planirostris possesses a plain snout that lacks any bony ornamentation or crests.
In contrast, the other species, M. westphali, features multiple bony crests along the upper jaw, particularly at the base and tip of the snout.
Researchers suggest that M. planirostris may have possessed soft tissue ornamentation, similar to keratinous crests known in other phytosaurs.
The tail makes up 51% of the total body length, making it longer than the rest of the body combined.
The inverted 'T' shape of chevrons at the tail end is unique to Mystriosuchus among phytosaurs but seen in sauropterygians and some crocodilians.
Mystriosuchus was first named by Eberhard Fraas in 1896.
The genus authority for Mystriosuchus is Fraas, 1896.
Its long jaws, similar to modern gharials, suggest a primarily fish-eating diet.
Microwear studies indicate a preference for softer invertebrates in addition to fish.
While originally thought to be freshwater, some specimens from Northern Italy indicate a completely marine lifestyle.
The genus includes two species: M. westphali and the type species M. planirostris.
Mystriosuchus is classified within the subfamily Pseudopalatinae.
Mystriosuchus belongs to the parent group Mystriosuchini.
Cladistic analysis later grouped Mystriosuchus with Pseudopalatinae instead of its former subfamily, Mystriosuchidae.
Christian Kammerer and colleagues synonymized Pseudopalatinae with Mystriosuchini because the latter has priority.
Mystriosuchus lived in Europe and Greenland during the Late Triassic (middle Norian).
Mystriosuchus lived from the Norian to the Hettangian, between 227.3 and 199.5 million years ago.
